actions.justification: Mandatory first step: patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes with planned contrast exposure. Hydration status assessment is critical to guide pre-procedure IV fluid administration to prevent contrast-induced nephropathy.
Mandatory: baseline eGFR must be established in this CKD stage 4 patient before contrast administration. eGFR will quantify renal function, risk-stratify for CIN, and guide contrast volume limits.

Mandatory: comprehensive risk factor review is required. This patient has two major CIN risk factors (CKD stage 4 + diabetes), which significantly elevate risk. Review may identify additional modifiable risk factors before the procedure.
Confirm current hemodynamic stability before contrast exposure in this CKD stage 4 diabetic patient undergoing cardiac catheterization.
Review current medications for nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, metformin, ACE inhibitors) that should be held or adjusted prior to contrast administration in a high-risk CKD patient.
Calculate the maximum safe contrast volume based on eGFR and body weight to minimize CI-AKI risk in this CKD stage 4 diabetic patient.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, both high risk factors for contrast-induced nephropathy. Evaluate whether alternative imaging (e.g., CO2 angiography, MRI) can be used instead of iodinated contrast to minimize nephrotoxin exposure before cardiac catheterization.

CKD stage 4 with diabetes places this patient at very high risk for contrast-induced AKI. Nephrology consultation is warranted to guide pre-procedural optimization, hydration strategy, and post-procedure monitoring.
Review and hold any concurrent nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, ACE inhibitors if appropriate) prior to contrast exposure in this high-risk CKD stage 4 diabetic patient.

Patient has CKD stage 4 with diabetes — documenting eGFR check is critical prior to contrast administration to establish baseline renal function and guide contrast-induced nephropathy prevention strategy.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy; discontinuing NSAIDs, metformin, and other nephrotoxic agents before cardiac catheterization is a guideline-recommended protective measure.
Monitoring urine output in this high-risk patient (CKD stage 4, diabetes) pre-procedure helps establish baseline renal perfusion status and guides pre-hydration strategy before contrast exposure.

Patient has diabetes and CKD stage 4 undergoing contrast administration. Metformin should be held prior to and after contrast exposure to prevent metformin-associated lactic acidosis, per standard guidelines.
IV crystalloid (isotonic saline) pre-hydration is a cornerstone of contrast-induced nephropathy prevention in high-risk patients with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization.
Post-contrast serum creatinine at 48 hours is recommended to detect contrast-induced AKI in this high-risk patient (CKD stage 4 + diabetes).
Patient has CKD stage 4; holding nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs) peri-procedurally reduces risk of contrast-induced nephropathy per CIN prevention guidelines.

Patient has diabetes and CKD stage 4 (likely eGFR <45, G3b or lower). Metformin should be held at time of contrast administration and withheld for 48h post-procedure to prevent lactic acidosis risk per ADA/KDIGO guidelines.
Post-contrast IV hydration with isotonic saline is a cornerstone of CIN prevention in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4 + diabetes). Plan should be confirmed prior to procedure.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, both major risk factors for contrast-induced nephropathy. Pre-procedure IV hydration (isotonic saline) is a cornerstone of CI-AKI prevention per guidelines and should be continued/confirmed prior to cardiac catheterization.
Ongoing urine output monitoring is essential in this high-risk CKD stage 4 diabetic patient to assess volume status and renal perfusion adequacy before contrast administration.
Serial serum creatinine monitoring at 48-72 hours post-contrast is standard of care for detecting contrast-induced AKI in high-risk patients with CKD and diabetes.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization is at high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Serial creatinine monitoring at 72 hours post-contrast is essential to detect AKI onset, as peak creatinine elevation from contrast nephropathy typically occurs at 48-72 hours.

Patient has CKD stage 4 (severely reduced eGFR) and diabetes, representing very high risk for contrast-induced AKI. Nephrology consultation is indicated for ongoing management guidance, consideration of pre/post hydration optimization, and planning for potential renal replacement therapy if needed.

Ongoing fluid optimization is a cornerstone of contrast nephropathy prevention in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4 + diabetes). Ensuring euvolemia before and after contrast administration minimizes renal ischemia and dilutes nephrotoxic contrast load.
